summary: This informational RFC discusses what value to use for the TCP Maximum Segment Size option. It updates RFC 879 and RFC 2385. It was replaced by RFC 9293.

eli5.summary: TCP carries data in chunks, and this explains how big a chunk should be when extra labels also take space.

questions: how is tcp mss calculated with options
what value for tcp maximum segment size option
does tcp mss account for ip options
subtitle: How to calculate the size of TCP data segments when IP and TCP options are present.

tldr.problem: When TCP uses options (such as timestamps or MD5 signatures), the original RFCs were unclear about how to adjust the Maximum Segment Size (MSS) option to account for those extra bytes. Different implementations made different choices, leading to packets that were either too small or too large.
tldr.mechanism: The MSS value announced during connection setup should account only for fixed IP and TCP header sizes, not variable options. The sender then reduces the actual data length in packets to account for any options it includes.
tldr.outcome: This clarification prevents IP fragmentation, ensures consistency across implementations, and updates RFC 879 and RFC 2385.

today: RFC 9293 is the current TCP specification and supersedes RFC 6691. The clear guidance on MSS calculation remains valid: use fixed header sizes only, and let the sender adjust for options.

sections.title: The Confusion About MSS and Options
sections.content:
The TCP Maximum Segment Size (MSS) option is announced when two computers establish a connection to tell each other the largest data payload they are willing to receive in a single packet. The original definition in RFC 879 states: 'The MSS counts only data octets in the segment, it does not count the TCP header or the IP header.'

This definition is ambiguous when options are involved. If the sender adds options like TCP timestamps or IP security fields, should the MSS be reduced to account for them? RFC 879 and RFC 2385 gave conflicting guidance, and implementations were inconsistent, sometimes leading to packets larger than the network path could handle without fragmentation.
sections.eli5: When you say 'send me chunks of 1400 bytes', do you mean 1400 bytes of data, or 1400 bytes total including the extra labels? The older RFCs were unclear.

sections.title: The Clear Rule
sections.content:
The MSS value announced in the connection setup should equal the effective Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) minus only the size of the fixed IP and TCP headers. For IPv4, that is 20 bytes each (40 total); for IPv6, it is 40 bytes for the IP header plus 20 for TCP (60 total). Do not reduce the MSS for any IP or TCP options that might be used.

Instead, the sender is responsible for reducing the actual data length in packets to account for any options it includes. This separation of concerns works because the sender knows which options it will use in each packet, while the receiver cannot know in advance. The goal is to prevent IP-level fragmentation, which happens when a packet exceeds the MTU of the network path.
sections.eli5: Tell the other side how much fits in a plain packet, with no labels. Then, when you add labels to your packets, make them smaller to fit.

sections.title: Why Sender Adjustment Is Better
sections.content:
Consider the consequence of the alternative: if the sender announced an MSS already reduced for options, and then did not include those options in a packet, the packet would be unnecessarily small, wasting bandwidth. Conversely, if the receiver did not know how many options the sender would use, it might send a response packet with options, making it larger than the advertised MSS, causing fragmentation.

A table in RFC 6691 illustrates this: only when the sender adjusts packet length for options and the MSS is not adjusted does everything work correctly. Since options are variable in length and the sender is the only one that knows what options will be included, the sender must be responsible for the adjustment.
sections.eli5: If you announce a smaller chunk size to account for labels you might add, and then don't use those labels, you waste space. The other side has no way to know. So you tell the truth about the plain size, then you handle your own labels.

sections.title: Exceptions and Path MTU Discovery
sections.content:
When an interface has variable MTU (such as with header compression that sometimes needs full headers and sometimes compressed headers), the sender should use the smallest effective MTU to calculate MSS, to avoid resynchronization problems in the compression layer.

IPv6 supports jumbograms (packets larger than 64K), so a received MSS value of 65,535 is treated as infinity, and Path MTU Discovery determines the actual limit. For avoiding fragmentation, implementations should use the smallest MTU on the connected network, not just the minimum 576-byte baseline. Setting MSS too small can also limit Path MTU Discovery's ability to find a larger path.
sections.eli5: If you're using compressed headers or jumbo packets, there are special rules. And if you set your chunk size too small, it can make the network think it can't send bigger packets later.

sections.title: Updates to Earlier RFCs
sections.content:
This RFC updates RFC 879 (which said to reduce MSS for IP options, which is incorrect) and RFC 2385 (which said to reduce MSS for the TCP MD5 option, which is also incorrect). The guidance here clarifies that neither of those claims are accurate: MSS should only reflect fixed header sizes.

This is an Informational RFC published in July 2012, later updated by RFC 9293.
sections.eli5: Two older RFCs gave wrong advice about this, and this one sets the record straight.
